sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows how to justify a modelling choice.

items.prompt: Find the mean and median of 4, 8, 6, 10, 2.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Decide what the quantities are before you compute anything.

items.prompt: A data set of five values between 10 and 30 has one additional reading of 233 appended. Which statement best describes the effect on the mean and the median?
choices: Neither statistic changes, because one value cannot affect a summary.
Both the mean and the median rise sharply.
The mean rises sharply while the median changes little, because the mean uses every value’s size.
The median rises sharply while the mean changes little.

items.prompt: A two-way table has row 1: 24 yes, 26 no; row 2: 18 yes, 17 no. Among row-1 respondents, what fraction answered yes?
A least-squares line for a data set is ŷ = 7x + 52, where x is measured in hour studieds and y in test points. Interpret the slope.
choices: The predicted value is 7 test points when x is 0.
Each additional hour studied is associated with an increase of about 7 test points.
Each additional hour studied causes an increase of exactly 7 test points.
Each additional test points is associated with 7 more hour studieds.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Plan in writing: what you will model, why that model, and how you will check it.

items.prompt: Towns with more fire engines report more fire damage. What conclusion is justified?
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
